title: The Return of the Beaver
subtitle: Britain's largest rodent is back after four centuries. Is the countryside ready for it?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For roughly four hundred years, the only beavers in Britain were in museums and place names. The Eurasian beaver, once common along the country's rivers, was hunted to extinction, prized for its fur, its meat and castoreum, a secretion used in medicine and perfume. By the sixteenth century it had almost certainly vanished. Its return, over the past two decades, has become one of the most closely watched and fiercely debated experiments in British conservation.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Part of the fascination lies in what beavers do. Few animals alter their surroundings so dramatically. Where a stream is too shallow to offer them protection, beavers build dams of branches, stones and mud, raising the water level until the entrances to their lodges and burrows lie safely underwater. Over time, a single straight channel can become a chain of ponds and side channels fringed by marsh. Ecologists describe beavers as 'ecosystem engineers' because the habitats they create are used by a great many other species: dragonflies, amphibians, fish, wading birds and bats are often more abundant at beaver sites than on comparable stretches of unaltered river.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The animals' return to Scotland took two very different routes. The first was official. In 2009 a small number of beavers brought over from Norway were released into Knapdale Forest in Argyll as part of the Scottish Beaver Trial, a five-year project run by conservation charities. The second was entirely unplanned. Even before the trial began, beavers had started to appear on the River Tay and its tributaries, almost certainly descended from animals that had escaped from private collections or been released illegally. The unofficial population grew faster and spread further than the official one, and it was partly the fact that beavers were already established in the wild that persuaded the Scottish Government, in 2016, to allow them to remain. Three years later they became a legally protected species in Scotland.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: England followed a similar path. In 2013 wild beavers were filmed on the River Otter in East Devon. Nobody knew where they had come from, and the government's initial response was to propose capturing them, partly because of the risk that they might carry disease. Local protests followed, and a compromise was eventually reached: the beavers would be tested for disease and, if healthy, returned to the river under a five-year study led by the Devon Wildlife Trust. When the River Otter Beaver Trial ended in 2020, the government announced that the animals could stay - the first time an extinct native mammal had been given official permission to live wild in England again.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Much of the scientific interest in Devon has focused on water. At a separate enclosed site in the west of the county, where a pair of beavers had been introduced in 2011, researchers from the University of Exeter measured the water entering and leaving an area of former farmland that the animals had dammed. They found that the ponds acted like a sponge. During heavy rain, water was held back and released more slowly, so that the peak flow downstream was lower and arrived later; in dry spells, the stored water continued to seep out, keeping the stream flowing. The dams also trapped large quantities of soil washed off nearby fields, together with some of the nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilisers that would otherwise have polluted the river.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Such findings have made beavers popular with advocates of 'natural flood management' - the idea that working with natural processes in the upper parts of a river catchment can reduce the risk of flooding in towns further downstream. Enthusiasts should be cautious, however. A few beaver ponds on a small stream cannot stop a major flood on a large river, where the volume of water is far greater than any dam could hold, and the effect of the animals depends heavily on the shape of the valley and the type of soil. Beavers are, at best, one tool among many, and their benefits are clearest at a local scale.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Not everyone welcomes the newcomers. Farmers, particularly those working low-lying land beside rivers, have raised a number of practical concerns. Dams can flood fields and block drainage ditches; burrows dug into riverbanks can weaken them until they collapse under the weight of a tractor; and beavers fell trees, including valuable orchard and woodland trees. In parts of Tayside, which contains some of the most productive arable land in Scotland, landowners have reported crops lost to waterlogging. Anglers, too, have worried that dams might prevent salmon and trout from reaching their spawning grounds, although the evidence on this point remains mixed.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The response has been to treat management as a normal part of living with the species. Problem dams can be lowered or removed, sometimes under licence; pipes can be inserted through a dam to hold water at an acceptable level; valuable trees can be protected with wire mesh or special paint; and in serious cases animals may be trapped and moved elsewhere. In Scotland, killing beavers is permitted only under licence and as a last resort. Supporters argue that the cost of such measures is modest compared with the public benefits beavers provide. Their opponents reply that those benefits are enjoyed by society as a whole, while the costs fall on a few landowners. How that balance is struck will decide whether the beaver remains a curiosity or becomes, once again, an ordinary part of the British countryside.
